text: Each and everyone of them agreed.
corrected: Each and every one of them agreed.

american.message: Use `each and every one` for referring to a group of people or things.

text: Alot of people came to the show.
corrected: A lot of people came to the show.

american.message: `a lot` should be written as two words.

fixed.american: A lot of people came to the show.

text: She don't like coffee.
corrected: She doesn't like coffee.

american.message: The form of the verb must agree in grammatical number with the pronoun.

fixed.american: She doesn't like coffee.

text: The cat licked it's paw.
corrected: The cat licked its paw.

american.message: Use the possessive pronoun `its` (without an apostrophe) to show ownership. The word `it's` (with an apostrophe) is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has' and should not be used to indicate possession.

fixed.american: The cat licked its paw.

text: Their going to the park later.
corrected: They're going to the park later.

american.message: Did you mean `they're`?

fixed.american: They're going to the park later.

text: I have went there before.
corrected: I have gone there before.

american.message: Use the past participle `gone` instead of `went` when using compound tenses or passive voice.

fixed.american: I have gone there before.

text: The book was wrote last year.
corrected: The book was written last year.

american.message: Use the past participle `written` instead of `wrote` when using compound tenses or passive voice.

fixed.american: The book was written last year.

text: He did it on accident.
corrected: He did it by accident.

american.message: Did you mean `by accident`?

fixed.american: He did it by accident.

text: This is suppose to be easy.
corrected: This is supposed to be easy.

american.message: Did you mean `supposed to`?

fixed.american: This is supposed to be easy.

text: We need to discuss about the budget.
corrected: We need to discuss the budget.

american.message: `About` is redundant

text: For all intensive purposes, the work is done.

american.message: The correct form is 'for all intents and purposes'.

fixed.american: For all intents and purposes, the work is done.

text: The submarine went bellow the surface.
corrected: The submarine went below the surface.

american.message: `Bellow` means to shout. You probably mean `below`.

fixed.american: The submarine went below the surface.

text: He was the one who eluded to the problem.
corrected: He was the one who alluded to the problem.

american.message: Did you mean `alluded to`?

fixed.american: He was the one who alluded to the problem.

text: The captain decided to change tact quickly.
corrected: The captain decided to change tack quickly.

american.message: A change in direction or approach is a change of `tack`. Not `tact` (or `tacks` or `tacts`).

fixed.american: The captain decided to change tack quickly.

text: We waited with baited breath.
corrected: We waited with bated breath.

american.message: Did you mean `bated breath`?

fixed.american: We waited with bated breath.

text: The the dog barked loudly.
corrected: The dog barked loudly.

american.message: Did you mean to repeat this word?

fixed.american: The dog barked loudly.

text: The results were very very good.
corrected: The results were very good.

american.message: Did you mean to repeat this word?

text: This is an useful tool.
corrected: This is a useful tool.

text: He is a honest worker.
corrected: He is an honest worker.

text: The app works well and no longer I need a manual.

text: Its a beautiful day outside.
corrected: It's a beautiful day outside.

american.message: Use `it's` (short for `it has` or `it is`) here, not the possessive `its`.

fixed.american: It's a beautiful day outside.

text: We had a really good time,thanks to you.
corrected: We had a really good time, thanks to you.

american.message: Use a space after a comma.

fixed.american: We had a really good time, thanks to you.

text: We bought bread , milk and eggs.
corrected: We bought bread, milk and eggs.

american.message: Don't use a space before a comma.

fixed.american: We bought bread, milk, and eggs.

text: i think the plan will work.
corrected: I think the plan will work.

american.message: The first-person singular subject pronoun must be capitalized.

fixed.american: I think the plan will work.

text: It is a  long road.
corrected: It is a long road.

american.message: There are 2 spaces where there should be only one.

fixed.american: It is a long road.

text: Where are you going ?
corrected: Where are you going?

american.message: Unnecessary space at the end of the sentence.

fixed.american: Where are you going?

text: This puzzle game is very addicting.
corrected: This puzzle game is very addictive.

american.message: When used as an adjective, `addictive` is the traditional and more f form.

fixed.american: This puzzle game is very addictive.

text: I could of done it better.
corrected: I could have done it better.

american.message: Use `have` rather than `of` here.

fixed.american: I could have done it better.

text: The new policy will effect everyone.
corrected: The new policy will affect everyone.

american.message: Use `affect` for the verb meaning to influence; `effect` usually names the result.

fixed.american: The new policy will affect everyone.

text: She is very unique in her approach.
corrected: She is very special in her approach.

american.message: `Unique` is absolute, so consider using `unique` alone or a more precise adjective such as `special`, `rare`, or `unusual`.

fixed.american: She is very special in her approach.

text: He is more taller than his brother.
corrected: He is taller than his brother.

american.message: Using `more` and the comparative form of the adjective together is redundant.

fixed.american: He is taller than his brother.

text: The meeting is at 3 PM in the afternoon.
corrected: The meeting is at 3 PM.

american.message: The time period is redundant because it repeats what's already specified by the AM/PM indicator.

fixed.american: The meeting is at 3 PM.
